paragraphs.text: These dragon pearls are made from Banzhang village leaf, from Menghai in Yunnan. The leaf was sorted to the gongting grade, which keeps only small buds. It was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition), then rolled by hand into pearls, one at a time.

Like all ripe pu’er, the buds went through [wet piling](shou:wet-piling). They were wetted and heaped so that heat, moisture and microbes could work on them. The pile was covered to hold in the heat the microbes make, and turned about once a week to spread it and let in air. It was kept below about 65°C, because hotter than that the leaf starts to char. Drinkers in Hong Kong and Guangdong once waited years for raw pu’er to darken with age, and the pile was developed to do that in weeks. So these pearls are ready to drink now, without years of waiting.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
